transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is trying to refocus voters' attention
after the stunning defection of his former Democratic primary opponent, Congresswoman
Hailey Stevens, yesterday.
We won't back down tomorrow, and we won't back down for the next six years because it
is our democracy, Selene, and we intend to use it.
After she endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers, Stevens was expelled from the state
party.
Michigan Democrats said the move energized voters.
Tens of millions of people have already voted.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro says polls tell us a lot of the races are going to be very close.
There was a new round of New York Times/Ciena polls out last night.
They were eye-popping.
They showed Democrats ahead by 11 in Michigan, seven in Texas, six in Maine, five in Kansas,
and Ohio.
A couple caveats, though.
This does not mean that that's what's going to happen.
First, not all of these showed Democrats at 50% in these polls, so there's a good number
of undecideds.
These polls also found that people who made up their minds in the last month sided with
Republicans by nine points.
And we should say that Michigan poll was before the feud between Democratic candidate Abdul
El-Sayed and his primary opponent, Congresswoman Hailey Stevens, who endorsed the Republican
in the race Mike Rogers on Sunday.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro reporting, "Congressional races may be getting a lot of the attention
this year, but more than 6,100 state legislative seats are also up for grabs," Carmen Russell
Slachanski of Member Station WHYY reports.
Republicans control legislatures in 28 states, while Democrats control 18.
Others are divided.
That GOP advantage stems from the 2010 midterms, when they swept state races.
However, Professor John Kennedy of Westchester University says that could change this year.
It's an opportunity for Democrats maybe to claw back some seats they've lost over the
years and perhaps even recapture some chambers.
Democrats spent millions on individual legislative races in states like Pennsylvania.
Where flipping the state Senate would give them power to implement elusive policy priorities,
such as a $15 minimum wage and increased public transit funding.
For NPR News, I'm Carmen Russell Slachanski in Philadelphia.
Federal investigators say parts of a business jet may have broken off before it crashed
in South Florida yesterday.
NPR's Joel Rose reports all nine people on board were killed.
Video recorded by witnesses captured the rapid nosedive and the fiery explosion on impact
near West Palm Beach.
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman says investigators are trying
to understand why the Learjet crashed on its way from Austin to the Bahamas.
We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact.
We're still seeking to determine that.
Chapman says the weather will be a major focus of the investigation, as one of the pilots
reported icy conditions at high altitude moments before the nosedive began.
Multiple media outlets reported that a 20-year-old Florida woman was one of the two pilots, though
NPR has not independently confirmed that.
Joel Rose, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes closed mixed today.
This is NPR.
Meta is delaying new terms for business accounts.
After backlash from media companies and open web advocates, the terms would allow Meta to
use automated tools to scrape data from business accounts.
Reports argue this could lead to Meta building competing services using the scraped content.
Meta insists the terms are about accurate product information, not news scraping.
A toothpaste that doesn't use fluoride is gaining popularity when it comes to dental
health.
NPR's Rachel Carlson reports on how it stacks up against traditional fluoride toothpaste.
The alternative toothpaste uses a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite.
It promises to help users prevent cavities, whiten teeth, reduce sensitivity, and strengthen
enamel — all without fluoride.
Early research on hydroxyapatite suggests it's effective, but studies are limited,
especially compared to decades of research on fluoride.
Dr. Livia Tanuta is a professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.
I would recommend it as the best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's
what we have a lot of evidence behind.
Health experts widely agree that fluoride is safe and helps prevent cavities.
It works best when you brush twice daily, floss, and visit your dentist regularly.
Rachel Carlson, NPR News.
The humble Dachshund is taking center stage in a new exhibition in Germany that explores
the history of the wiener dog in art.
Dachshund owners Pablo Picasso, David Hockney, and Andy Warhol are among the artists featured
in the show.
I'm Ryland Barton, you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from CURE Alzheimer's Fund.
From family to community, connections and the memories they make are everything.
CURE Alzheimer's Fund empowers scientists pursuing bold Alzheimer's research.
Learn more at curealz.org.

topics.text: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed responds to Congresswoman Hailey Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers
New York Times/Siena polls show Democrats leading in Michigan, Texas, Maine, Kansas, and Ohio
State legislative races across 6,100 seats are up for grabs, with Democrats targeting Pennsylvania
Investigators say parts of a Learjet broke off before it crashed near West Palm Beach, killing nine
Meta delays new business account terms that would let it scrape data amid media backlash
Non-fluoride hydroxyapatite toothpaste gains popularity, but experts still recommend fluoride toothpaste
Dachshund-themed exhibition in Germany explores the wiener dog's role in art history
